title: Steady passage
excerpt: Bulk and liquid cargo move on relationships as much as on routes. How the shipping arm thinks about reliability when conditions at sea and in the market rarely agree.
body: Shipping is a business of things not going to plan. Weather moves, ports congest, and a market can reprice between the moment a cargo is agreed and the moment it is loaded. Anyone who has been in it long enough has stopped expecting otherwise.

What is left, once you accept that, is the question of how you behave when conditions turn. The commercially optimal move in any single instance is often to renegotiate. The trouble is that counterparties remember, and the next negotiation begins from what you did last time.

The group has generally taken the other position: turn up on the agreed terms in a bad month, and accept that this costs something. It is not sentiment. A counterparty who knows how you behave under pressure removes a category of risk from their own planning, and that is worth more over several years than a better rate taken once.
The result is fewer relationships, held longer. It is a slower way to build a book and it produces a business that is considerably easier to run when nothing is cooperating.
